title: Why you forget what you came in for
teaser: Walked into a room and forgot why? In a 2011 study, walking through a doorway made people more likely to forget an object they had just handled.

slides.alt: Reel cover: Brain Glitch. Walked into a room and forgot why? Blame the doorway.

body: Walked into a room and forgot why? Blame the doorway.

In a 2011 study, 55 people moved objects from table to table through a set of virtual rooms. Asked about an object they had just carried or set down, they got it wrong 12% of the time after crossing one large room, and 19% of the time just after walking through a doorway, over the same distance.

The researchers' explanation: a doorway is an event boundary. Your brain updates its model of what's going on, and the last event gets harder to reach. In a later experiment, walking back into the first room didn't help.
Send this to someone who always forgets why they came in.
forDesigners: Breaks between screens and sections work like doorways. Restate the goal on the far side of one.

sources.label: Radvansky, G.A., Krawietz, S.A. & Tamplin, A.K. (2011). Walking through doorways causes forgetting: Further explorations. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 64(8), 1632–1645. Experiment 1, Table 1; Experiment 3.
